headline: Bishkek links haulage e-permits with six countries; Irad's lorries, on Kyrgyz paper, have none
dek: The ISEZ is not recognised, so no body here can issue or receive an interstate permit, and the Kyrgyz Border Service counted 17 seizures on the China road this year.
paragraphs: A Kyrgyz trade-facilitation official said this week that Bishkek is linking its electronic haulage permit system, e-Permit, with six countries, to cut paperwork, speed customs checks and build transport corridors. Irad is not one of the six. Because it is not a recognised state, no body in the Irad Special Economic Zone can issue an interstate haulage permit, and none abroad can accept one from here.

The practical result is already on the road. Irad's export lorries run on Kyrgyz plates and on paper issued through Kyrgyz-registered companies, the pattern Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics has used for years. ISEZ plates, issued by the Republican Gendarmerie's Highway Patrol Corps, are not recognised in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan or Kyrgyzstan.

The Customs Service said it clears freight on the documents a driver presents, and that haulage permits are not its business. "We inspect what arrives at our posts and we release it against the papers it carries," Director Uson Yakupov told the Herald. "A permit for the other side of the line is for the other side to give." The service handles most road freight toward Kazakhstan at the Talas Customs Clearance Terminal and the Talas North Terminal. The Ministry of Transport, which sets roads and haulage policy, had not replied to written questions by deadline.

Trans-Chuy's executive director, Ilyas Sarsenbayev, said the company's lorries follow the Kyrgyz arrangement because there is no other. "The cargo is Iradi, the plate and the permit are Kyrgyz," he said. "If Bishkek's system joins up with more neighbours, our trucks pass through it as Kyrgyz trucks, which is how they pass now." He declined to say what the arrangement costs the company. Trans-Chuy Terminal Services LLC, registered in Nurzhan in March 2019 (Register of Firms NZ-19-002207), runs the bonded warehouses at the Talas North Terminal.

Smaller hauliers describe the cost more plainly. Anvar Tojiboev, who drives a Kyrgyz-registered tractor unit out of Bazar-Korgon, said he pays a forwarding agent in Jalal-Abad for each trip and cannot name the company that holds his permit. "If the agent's licence is suspended, my truck stops, and I have no one in Talas to complain to," he said. The Herald could not verify his figures for the agent's fee, and the fee is not in any published tariff.

The Kyrgyz frontier offers no fallback. The ISEZ has no border arrangement with Kyrgyzstan, and its crossings at Suzak and Kichi-Korgon work informally. The February 2025 memorandum with Uzbekistan set shared customs hours at the main crossings near Bazar-Korgon and Tash-Kömür, where lorries cross at Kyzyl-Tuu, but it is a memorandum on trade and border coordination, not a permit scheme, and Tashkent says it implies no recognition.

Trade on the China road is where the missing paper shows most. The Kyrgyz Border Service counted 17 seizures on it in 2026 and, in its own words, no arrests on the ISEZ side. A Kyrgyz veterinary and phytosanitary desk at the Talas Airport Logistics Hub, beside the Iradiya terminal, certifies exports from the ISEZ on Kyrgyz paper, so Kyrgyzstan collects fees on both.

Prof. Raisa Akmatova, an economist at Talas State University, said the permit gap is a cost that never appears in a budget line. "Every step done in Bishkek's name is a margin paid to someone in Bishkek," she said. "Add a day's delay at a crossing with no agreement, and the exporter bears it, not the state." She said no one has published a figure for the total.

Nothing in the Kyrgyz announcement suggests a change for Irad. The six linked countries were not named to the Herald, and no date was given for when the system would be running across all of them. Hauliers here will keep using the paper they have.
